summary:
South Sumatra stands under the national framework of Indonesia, a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that South Sumatra, alongside Aceh, criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, alongside national provisions targeting morality. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and reach anyone present in that province, including foreign visitors; two men were publicly caned there for a same-sex relationship in February 2025.

Enforcement elsewhere takes the form of venue raids. On 22 June 2025 Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

A trans traveller has died in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call, his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Official policy frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. Presidential Regulation No. 111 of 2025, issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025, sets the national defence policy for 2025 to 2029 and lists the "spread of LGBTQ culture" among non-military threats. ABC News reporting of 15 August 2026 ties that framing to violence, recording 10 attacks on trans women in Bogor between 30 March and 15 July 2026 and 45 victim-survivors according to advocacy group data, with victims punched, kicked and in some cases stripped. An official quoted in the same reporting insists the regulation is a broader defence policy not aimed at LGBTQI people.

Within South Sumatra, Palembang's city government announced on 19 July 2026 that it is preparing a regulation rejecting LGBT, presented as local follow-through on Perpres No. 111 of 2025. Mayor Ratu Dewa made the announcement in the courtyard of the Grand Mosque. The regulation remains in preparation rather than enacted, specifies no penalty, and no enforcement event is documented for the province.

OutRight Action International's mapping of discriminatory regional regulations across eight Indonesian provinces includes South Sumatra, placing the province inside the regional-bylaw belt from which drafts such as Palembang's extend.
tangentialFactors:
The national and local layers move together but are not identical in force. Perpres No. 111 of 2025 operates at national level and is cited explicitly by Palembang's city government as the basis for its own draft, so a visitor should expect provincial and municipal instruments to be justified in the language of national defence policy rather than of criminal law.

Public corporal punishment remains geographically confined. The caning of two men in February 2025 was imposed under Aceh's provincial religious law and applies to anyone present in Aceh; the sources do not describe an equivalent regime in South Sumatra.

Violence against trans women has been documented at scale in other provinces during the same period as Palembang's announcement. The 10 attacks in Bogor between 30 March and 15 July 2026, and the 45 victim-survivors reported by an advocacy group, indicate a countrywide climate rather than a South Sumatra-specific pattern.

Local security apparatus has acted against trans women in neighbouring provinces. Reporting carried in the previous record for this jurisdiction cites a Satpol PP raid on three trans women in Lampung in November 2018, an example of the municipal enforcement pattern that the OutRight mapping documents across the Sumatran belt.

Airport and drug-charges exposure carries a distinct and documented risk for foreign nationals. The 2022 death of Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla in custody shows that trans travellers face the general hazards of Indonesian detention as well as those arising from identity-based provisions.

South Sumatra appears in OutRight Action International's 'Creeping Criminalisation' mapping of discriminatory regional regulations in eight Indonesian provinces, which documents the province's position among local bylaws that restrict the lives of LGBTQ+ residents.

Residents are directly exposed to the national provisions recorded by the Human Dignity Trust country profile, which names South Sumatra as one of two provinces criminalising same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, alongside morality provisions in the national penal code.

The Human Dignity Trust profile also records the Puncak villa raid of 22 June 2025, in which 75 people were arrested after a privately rented gathering was reported as a "gay party"; Amnesty International stated the gathering violated no law.

Perpres No. 111 of 2025 places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as non-military threats to be monitored and controlled. Reporting from August 2026 links that framing to attacks on trans women, while an official quoted by ABC News maintains the regulation is a broader defence policy rather than a measure aimed at LGBTQI people.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not state what penalty, if any, applies under a South Sumatra provincial or municipal bylaw to same-sex conduct; the Human Dignity Trust profile identifies the province as criminalising such conduct but no named statute, penalty range, or prosecution record for South Sumatra is supplied here. That gap is unresolved rather than settled either way.

Whether the Palembang regulation has been enacted after 19 July 2026 is unresolved. The only sourced status is that it was in preparation with no penalty specified and no enforcement documented.

No enforcement event in South Sumatra itself is documented in this inventory. The raid, the caning and the reported attacks on trans women all occurred in other provinces and are used as evidence of the national environment.

The figure of 45 victim-survivors alongside the 10 attacks in Bogor derives from advocacy group data cited by ABC News and is not independently corroborated by a second source in this inventory.

An official quoted by ABC News disputes the reading that Perpres No. 111 of 2025 targets LGBTQI people, describing it as a broader defence policy. The sources do not resolve whether the regulation has direct legal effect on private conduct or operates as framing for local instruments.
